George Best (22 May 1946 – 25 November 2005) was a Northern Irish professional footballer who played as a right winger, spending most of his club career at Manchester United. A skillful dribbler, he is considered one of the greatest players of all time,[3][4] along with being considered one of the most talented to play.[5][6] He was named European Footballer of the Year in 1968 and came fifth in the FIFA Player of the Century vote. Best received plaudits for his playing style, which combined pace, skill, balance, feints, the ability to get past defenders and goalscoring. In 1999 he was on the six-man shortlist for the BBC's Sports Personality of the Century. He was an inaugural inductee into the English Football Hall of Fame in 2002.
Born in Belfast, Best began his club career in England with Manchester United, with the scout who had spotted his talent at the age of 15 sending a telegram to manager Matt Busby which read: "I think I've found you a genius". After making his debut at age 17, he scored 179 goals in 470 appearances over 11 years and was the club's top goalscorer in the league for five consecutive seasons.[7] He won two League titles, two Charity Shields and the European Cup with the club.
In international football, Best was capped 37 times for Northern Ireland between 1964 and 1977. A combination of the team's performance and his lack of fitness in 1982 meant that he never played in the finals of a major tournament. He considered his international career as being "recreational football", with the expectations placed on a smaller nation in Northern Ireland being much less than with his club. He is regarded as one of the greatest players never to have played at a World Cup. The Irish Football Association described him as the "greatest player to ever pull on the green shirt of Northern Ireland".[8]

With his good looks, dark Beatle mop-top hair and playboy lifestyle, Best became one of the first media celebrity footballers, earning the nickname "o Quinto Beatle" by Portuguese press reporters after a stand-out performance for Manchester United in Lisbon in March 1966. However, his extravagant lifestyle led to various personal problems, most notably alcoholism, from which he suffered for the rest of his life. These issues affected him on and off the field, often causing controversy.[9] Although conscious of his problems, he made light of them and was known for his intelligence and wit on the subject during periods of sobriety: "I spent a lot of money on booze, girls and fast cars – the rest I just squandered".[10] After football, he spent some time as a football analyst, but his financial and health problems continued into his retirement. He died in 2005, aged 59, from complications from the immunosuppressive drugs he needed to take after a liver transplant in 2002.
Early years and familyedit  
Best grew up on the Cregagh estate, east Belfast. The playing fields in the estate where he played football as a boy, Cregagh Green, is protected for community recreation in perpetuity as a Fields in Trust Active Space.[11]
George Best was born on 22 May 1946 in Belfast, the first child of Richard "Dickie" Best (1919–2008) and Anne Withers (1922–1978). He was raised in the Cregagh estate in east Belfast. Best had five siblings: four sisters, Carol, Barbara, Julie, and Grace, and one brother, Ian Busby Best.[12] Best's mother, herself an Irish hockey international, recalled that the boy was able to stand aged ten months and from then on was never seen without a ball at his feet, even taking one to bed.[13] His father was a member of the Orange Order and as a boy George carried the strings of the banner in his local Cregagh lodge. In his autobiography, Best mentioned how important the Order was to his family.[14] The Best family was raised in the Free Presbyterian faith.[15]

In 1957, the academically gifted Best passed the 11-plus and went to Grosvenor High School, but he soon played truant as the school specialised in rugby union. Best then moved to Lisnasharragh Secondary School, reuniting him with friends from primary school and allowing him to focus on football. He played for Cregagh Boys Club.[16] He grew up supporting Glentoran and Wolverhampton Wanderers.[17]
Anne Best died from alcoholism-related cardiovascular disease in 1978, at the age of 55.[18] Best's father died on 16 April 2008, 3 years after George's death, at the age of 88, in the Ulster Hospital in Dundonald, Northern Ireland.[19]
Club careeredit  
Manchester Unitededit
At the age of 15, Best was discovered in Belfast by Manchester United scout Bob Bishop, whose telegram to United manager Matt Busby read: "I think I've found you a genius."[20][21] His local club Glentoran had previously rejected him for being "too small and light".[22] Best was subsequently given a trial and signed up by United's chief scout Joe Armstrong. His first time moving to the club, Best quickly became homesick and stayed for only two days before going back home to Northern Ireland.[23] He returned to Manchester and spent two years as an amateur, as English clubs were not allowed to take Northern Irish players on as apprentices. He was given a job as an errand boy on the Manchester Ship Canal, allowing him to train with the club twice a week.[24]
Best made his First Division debut, aged 17, on 14 September 1963 against West Bromwich Albion at Old Trafford in a 1–0 victory.[25] He then dropped back into the reserves, before scoring his first goal for the first team in his second appearance in a 5–1 win over Burnley on 28 December.[25] Manager Matt Busby then kept Best in the team; by the end of the 1963–64 season, he had made 26 appearances, scoring six goals. Manchester United finished second, four points behind Liverpool.[26]

They reached the semi-finals of the FA Cup, where a defeat to West Ham United cost Best the chance to break a record. In the final Preston North End's Howard Kendall became the youngest ever player in a FA Cup Final – he shared the same birth date as Best.[26] That same season, Best captained the Manchester United side that won the 1964 FA Youth Cup, the sixth FA Youth Cup won under the management of Jimmy Murphy and the first since the 1958 Munich air disaster.[27]
The United Trinity statue of Best (left), Denis Law (centre) and Bobby Charlton (right) outside Old Trafford  
Rear view looking towards the stadium
Though opponents would often use rough play to try to stifle his technical ability, Busby ensured that "fierce, sometimes brutal" training sessions left Best well used to coping with tough challenges.[28] In the 1964–65 season, his first full season as a first team regular, Best helped Manchester United to claim the league title.[29] A 1–0 victory at Elland Road proved decisive as the title race came down to goal average between the "Red Devils" and bitter rivals Leeds United. Leeds managed to gain some measure of revenge though, by knocking Manchester United out of the FA Cup at the semi-final stage.[29] Over the course of the campaign Best contributed 14 goals in 59 competitive games.[29] He scored the opening goal of the 1965 FA Charity Shield at Old Trafford, which ended in a 2–2 draw with Liverpool.[30]
The rising star of English football, Best was catapulted to superstar status at the age of 19, when he scored two goals in a European Cup quarter-final match against Benfica at the Estádio da Luz on 9 March 1966.[31] His impressive stand-out display allied with his dark Beatle mop-top hair, the Portuguese media dubbed him "O Quinto Beatle" ("the fifth Beatle"); on the team's return to England, Best was photographed on the airport tarmac in his new sombrero with the headline, "El Beatle".[32][31] His talent and showmanship made him a crowd and media favourite and he went from being headline news in the back pages to the front pages.[31]

Before the game, manager Matt Busby had told his wingers, Best and Connelly, to stay deep for the first 20 minutes. Keep it tight and quieten the crowd. But George Best was only 19, too young for such caution. All he heard was 'blah, blah, blah'. When the game started, he grabbed it by the scruff. 'Watch this, Eusebio. And Coluna, Simoes, Torres, Germano, Jose Augusto. I'm George Best, and this is how it's done.'
— 'El Beatle' arrives, Jon Carter for ESPN.[32]
Other nicknames included the "Belfast Boy", while he was often referred to as "Geordie" in his native Belfast and "Georgie" in England.[33] However United failed to win any major honours in the 1965–66 season. Best was injured from 26 March onwards, with a twisted knee following a bad tackle from a Preston North End player.[34] United staff claimed it was light ligament damage, to keep Best on the field for the rest of the campaign.[34] He had little faith in the United medical staff and so he secretly saw Glentoran's physiotherapist, who readjusted his ligaments in a painful procedure.[35] His last game of the season, his knee strapped-up, came on 13 April, a 2–0 defeat to Partizan Belgrade at Partizan Stadium.[36]
The 1966–67 season was again successful, as Manchester United claimed the league title by four points. Best stated that "if the championship was decided on home games we would win it every season. This time our away games made the difference. We got into the right frame of mind."[37] An ever-present all season long, he scored 10 goals in 45 games. He then helped the "Red Devils" to share the Charity Shield with a 3–3 draw with FA Cup winners Tottenham Hotspur. It was the first game to be broadcast in colour on British television.[38]

Best scored twice against rivals Liverpool in a 2–0 win at Anfield and claimed a hat-trick against Newcastle United in a 6–0 home win on the penultimate league game of the season. However a home defeat to local rivals Manchester City proved costly, as City claimed the league title with a two-point lead over United. Yet the 1967–68 season was remembered by United fans for the European Cup win. After disposing of Maltese Hibernians, United advanced past Yugoslavian Sarajevo with a 2–1 home win. Best assisted John Aston for the first and scored the second himself and was described by Geoffrey Green of The Times as "the centrepiece of the chessboard ... a player full of fantasy; a player who lent magic to what might have been whimsy".[39]
In the quarter-finals, United advanced past Polish club Górnik Zabrze 2–1 on aggregate, having held on to their aggregate lead in freezing temperatures in front of 105,000 at Silesian Stadium. Despite losing the away tie 1–0, Best described the defeat as "one of our best-ever performances, given all the unwelcome circumstances".[40] Facing six times champions Real Madrid in the semi-finals, Best scored the only goal of the home fixture with a 15-yard strike that Alex Stepney described as one of Best's finest goals.[41] In the tie at the Bernabéu, Best was marked effectively by Manuel Sanchís Martínez, but on the one time Best got the better of him he made a telling pass[42] to Bill Foulkes, who calmly found the net,[43] to level the game at 3–3 and to win the aggregate tie 4–3.[44]

In an interview, Manchester United's Alex Stepney said: "Best would knock the ball on to the goalkeeper's shin, who would be rushing towards this feet to close down the angle, and the ball would bounce back to him and he would score. No one has been able to emulate that in football. Not only did he do it in training but he did it against Manchester United's arch rivals Liverpool at Anfield."[104]
The National Football Museum noted that Best played in an era of muddy pitches and heavy tackling, yet appeared to "glide through opponents" and could play on either wing, as a forward, or behind a central striker.[105] Writing for These Football Times, Jon Townsend highlighted Best's balance, strength on the ball, finishing and ability to slalom through defences, and argued that his game would have translated well to the modern era despite his having played without modern advantages such as sports science, nutrition, manicured pitches and lighter boots.[106] In a 2015 interview, José Mourinho, then manager of Chelsea, named Best as the player from any era he would most like to sign, describing him as "amazing" and "30 years ahead of his time".[107]
Personal lifeedit  
George Best's voice  
from the BBC Radio 4 programme The New Elizabethans, 20 July 2012[108]  
Problems playing this file? See media help.
During his early years at Old Trafford, Best was a shy teenager who passed his free time in snooker halls.[109] However, he later became known for his long hair, good looks and extravagant celebrity lifestyle, and he appeared on Top of the Pops in 1965.[110]
In 1969 Eva Haraldsted sued him for breach of promise, in the last such prominent case in England. However, the case never reached trial; instead, Haraldsted received a settlement of £500.[111]
Best had a brief relationship with actress Sinéad Cusack in 1971.[112]

He opened a nightclub called Slack Alice on Bootle Street in Manchester in 1973 and owned restaurants in the city including Oscars, on the site of the old Waldorf Hotel.[113][114] He also owned fashion boutiques, in partnership with Manchester City player Mike Summerbee. Best's cousin, Gary Reid, a member of the Ulster Defence Association, was killed in 1974 during an episode of serious rioting in east Belfast.[115]
"In 1969 I gave up women and alcohol—it was the worst 20 minutes of my life."
— Best quips on his lifestyle.[116]
Best married Angela MacDonald-Janes on 24 January 1978 at Candlelight Wedding Chapel in Las Vegas, having met her in the United States when Best was playing for the Los Angeles Aztecs in 1976. Their son, Calum, was born in 1981. They separated in 1982 and divorced in 1986.[117]
"If I had to choose between dribbling past five players and scoring from 40 yards at Anfield or shagging Miss World, it'd be a hard choice. Thankfully, I've done both."
— Best on life on and off the field.[118]
He married Alex Pursey in 1995 in Kensington and Chelsea, London.[119] They divorced in 2004[120] with no children. In 2004, she alleged that Best was violent towards her at times during their marriage, an issue that was covered in Best's authorised 1998 biography Bestie in which Alex claimed that Best punched her in the face on more than one occasion.[121] Earlier in the book it is revealed that he struck another of his girlfriends at least once and was arrested and charged with assault on a waitress, Stevie Sloniecka, in November 1972, when he fractured her nose in Reuben's nightclub, Manchester.[122] He was successfully defended when the case reached court in January 1973 by barrister George Carman QC, a close drinking companion of Best, as acknowledged in his book, Scoring at Half Time.

Although the football pitch was his arena, Best was essentially a pop star—young, stylish, strikingly beautiful, possessed of a creative confidence that bordered on arrogance, and worshipped by young men and women alike. Like The Beatles and The Rolling Stones, he epitomised the first, sudden, dynamic emergence of a postwar youth culture that, for better or worse, would help define the rest of the century. Long before Beckham, he was Britain's first footballer as popular icon.
— Sean O'Hagan in The Guardian on Best's celebrity status in the 1960s.[123]
At the peak of his career in the late 1960s and early 1970s, Best advertised Cookstown sausages on television with the phrase "the Best family sausages".[124] In 2007 a memorial plaque was placed outside the pork factory in the County Tyrone town.[124] In the early 1970s, Best also advertised eggs, under the campaign "E for B and Georgie Best", both in print and on TV, where "E for B" was short for "Eggs for Breakfast".[125]
Best had a cameo as himself in the 1971 British comedy film Percy. In 1984, he made a fitness album with Mary Stävin called Shape Up and Dance. The Farm's video for their 1992 cover version of The Human League's "Don't You Want Me" featured Best mouthing the chorus.[126] A biographical film entitled Best was released in May 2000, with John Lynch portraying George Best. Indie rock band The Wedding Present named their first album George Best and featured him on the cover wearing his red Manchester United kit. After his death, Brian Kennedy and Peter Corry released a single entitled George Best – A Tribute. Best features in EA Sports' FIFA video game series; he was included as an icon in the FIFA 19 Ultimate Team Legends.[127]

In 2007, GQ magazine named him as one of the 50 most stylish men of the past 50 years.[128] When Best played football, salaries were a fraction of what top players earn today, but, with his pop star image and celebrity status, Best still earned a fortune. He lost almost all of it. When asked what happened to the money he had earned, Best quipped: "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds (women) and fast cars. The rest I just squandered."[129]
In 2012, Best was featured in the list of The New Elizabethans to mark the diamond Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II. A panel of seven academics, journalists and historians named Best among the group of people in the UK "whose actions during the reign of Elizabeth II have had a significant impact on lives in these islands and given the age its character".[108]
Alcoholismedit
"I was born with a great gift, and sometimes with that comes a destructive streak. Just as I wanted to outdo everyone when I played, I had to outdo everyone when we were out on the town."
— Best on his excesses off the field.[130]
Best suffered from alcoholism for most of his adult life, leading to numerous controversies and, eventually, his death.[131] In 1981, while playing in the United States, Best stole from a woman by taking money from her handbag to fund a drinking session. He recalled the incident, "We were sitting in a bar on the beach, and when she got up to go to the toilet I leaned over and took all the money she had in her bag."[132]
In 1984, Best received a three-month prison sentence for drunk driving, assaulting a police officer and failing to answer bail. He spent Christmas 1984 at Ford Open Prison. Contrary to popular belief and urban legend, he never played football for the prison team. In September 1990, Best appeared on the primetime BBC1 chat show Wogan in which he was heavily drunk and swore, at one point saying to the host, "Terry, I like screwing".[133] In 2002, he told The Guardian: "I was ill and everyone could see it but me."[123]

Liver transplant and controversyedit
Best was diagnosed with severe liver damage in March 2000.[134] His liver was said to be functioning at only 20%.[135][136] In 2001, he was admitted to hospital with pneumonia.[137] At the end of July and start of August 2002, he had a successful liver transplant at the private Cromwell Hospital in London.[134] He haemorrhaged so badly during the operation that he nearly died.[138] The transplant was performed at public expense on the NHS, a decision which was controversial due to Best's alcoholism.[139] The controversy was reignited in 2003 when he was spotted openly drinking white wine spritzers.[131] On 2 February 2004, Best was convicted of another drink-driving offence and banned from driving for 20 months.[140]
Deathedit  
Gates of Belfast City Hall soon after Best's death, Another view.
Best continued to drink and was sometimes seen at his local pub in Surbiton, London. On 3 October 2005, he was admitted to intensive care at the private Cromwell Hospital in London, suffering from a kidney infection caused by the side effects of immuno-suppressive drugs used to prevent his body from rejecting his transplanted liver.[134] On 27 October, newspapers stated that Best was close to death and had sent a farewell message to his loved ones. Close friends in the game visited his bedside to make their farewells, including Rodney Marsh, Bobby Charlton and Denis Law.[141]
On 20 November, the tabloid News of the World published a picture of Best, at his own request, showing him in his hospital bed with jaundice, along with a warning about the dangers of alcohol with his message: 'Don't die like me'.[141] In the early hours of 25 November 2005, treatment was stopped; later that day he died, aged 59, as a result of a lung infection and multiple organ failure.[134][142]

Tributes were paid to Best from around the world, including from arguably three of the greatest football players ever, Pelé, Diego Maradona and Johan Cruyff.[95] British prime minister Tony Blair described him as "probably the most naturally gifted footballer of his generation, one of the greatest footballers the UK has ever produced".[143] Maradona commented: "George inspired me when I was young. He was flamboyant and exciting and able to inspire his teammates. I actually think we were very similar players – dribblers who were able to create moments of magic."[95] Fellow Manchester United legend Eric Cantona also paid tribute, saying: "I would love him to save me a place in his team, George Best that is, not God."[144] At Best's funeral, the Duke of York sent white roses bearing a message which described him as "an inspirational footballer from Northern Ireland whose skills captured the imagination of fans from around the world".[145]
The Premier League announced that a minute's silence would be observed before all Premier League games to be held over the weekend of his death; however, at many grounds a minute's applause broke out in his honour.[146] The first match at Old Trafford after Best's death was a League Cup tie against West Bromwich Albion, the club against which he made his debut for Manchester United in 1963.[147] The match, which United won, was preceded by tributes from former teammate Sir Bobby Charlton. Best's son, Calum, former teammates and surviving members from the West Brom team which he played against in his debut all joined the current United squad on the pitch for a minute's silence. During this, fans in every seat held aloft pictures of Best, which were given out before the match.[147]
Funeraledit  
The Best family grave at Roselawn Cemetery, overlooking east Belfast

His body left the family home at Cregagh Road, East Belfast, shortly after 10 am on Saturday 3 December 2005. The cortege then travelled the short distance to Stormont. The route was lined with around 100,000 mourners.[148] Former Northern Ireland manager Billy Bingham, international teammates Derek Dougan, Peter McParland, Harry Gregg and Gerry Armstrong and Denis Law were the first to carry the coffin to the base of the Stormont steps.[148]
There was an 11 am service in the Grand Hall attended by 300 invited guests relayed to around 25,000 mourners inside the grounds of Stormont. Best's brother Ian, agent Phil Hughes, Dr Akeel Alisa, who treated Best, and his brothers-in-law Norman McNarry and Alan McPherson, were also pallbearers. As the cortege left Stormont, the Gilnahirk pipe band played. The funeral was live on several television stations including BBC One. Afterwards, Best was interred beside his mother, Annie Mary Best, in a private ceremony at the hill-top Roselawn Cemetery, overlooking east Belfast.[148]
Memorialsedit  
Following his death, the George Best Belfast City Airport was named after him  
George Best waxwork in Malahide, Dublin
Belfast City Airport was renamed George Best Belfast City Airport as a tribute to Best.[149][150] The official new name and signage was unveiled to a gathering of the Best family and friends at the airport on 22 May 2006, which would have been his 60th birthday. Public opinion in Northern Ireland about the renaming of the airport was divided, with one poll showing 52% in favour and 48% against.[151] Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) deputy leader and East Belfast Member of Parliament Peter Robinson, in whose constituency Belfast City airport is situated, stated that his preference was a sports stadium be named after Best.[152]
"With feet as sensitive as a pickpocket's hands, his control of the ball under the most violent pressure was astonishing. The bewildering repertoire of feints and swerves... and balance that would have made Isaac Newton decide he might as well have eaten the apple."
— Sports writer Hugh McIlvanney.[100]

In March 2006, the airline Flybe named a Dash 8 (Q400) plane The George Best. The aircraft was later used to carry Best's family across to the Manchester memorial service for Best.[153]
In June 2006, Sarah Fabergé, great-granddaughter of Russian imperial jeweller Peter Carl Fabergé, was commissioned to create the George Best Egg, in tribute. A limited edition of 68 eggs were produced, with all profits from the sale of the eggs going to the George Best Foundation, which promotes health through sport and supports people with alcohol and drug problems.[154] The first egg is on display at the George Best Airport. For the first anniversary of his death, Ulster Bank issued 1 million commemorative £5 notes.[155] The notes sold out in five days.[156] The notes sold on the online auction site eBay for up to £30.[157]
In December 2006, the George Best Memorial Trust launched a fund-raising drive to raise £200,000 in subscriptions to pay for a life-size bronze sculpture of George Best. By 2008 the money had still not been raised until a local developer, Doug Elliott, announced on 29 January 2008, that he would put up the rest of the money and would manage delivery of the project.[158]

texts.2:
George Best (22 May 1946 – 25 November 2005) was a Northern Irish professional footballer who played as a right winger, spending most of his club career at Manchester United. A skillful dribbler, he is considered one of the greatest players of all time,[3][4] along with being considered one of the most talented to play.[5][6] He was named European Footballer of the Year in 1968 and came fifth in the FIFA Player of the Century vote. Best received plaudits for his playing style, which combined pace, skill, balance, feints, the ability to get past defenders and goalscoring. In 1999 he was on the six-man shortlist for the BBC's Sports Personality of the Century. He was an inaugural inductee into the English Football Hall of Fame in 2002.
Born in Belfast, Best began his club career in England with Manchester United, with the scout who had spotted his talent at the age of 15 sending a telegram to manager Matt Busby which read: "I think I've found you a genius". After making his debut at age 17, he scored 179 goals in 470 appearances over 11 years and was the club's top goalscorer in the league for five consecutive seasons.[7] He won two League titles, two Charity Shields and the European Cup with the club.
In international football, Best was capped 37 times for Northern Ireland between 1964 and 1977. A combination of the team's performance and his lack of fitness in 1982 meant that he never played in the finals of a major tournament. He considered his international career as being "recreational football", with the expectations placed on a smaller nation in Northern Ireland being much less than with his club. He is regarded as one of the greatest players never to have played at a World Cup. The Irish Football Association described him as the "greatest player to ever pull on the green shirt of Northern Ireland".[8]
texts.3:
With his good looks, dark Beatle mop-top hair and playboy lifestyle, Best became one of the first media celebrity footballers, earning the nickname "o Quinto Beatle" by Portuguese press reporters after a stand-out performance for Manchester United in Lisbon in March 1966. However, his extravagant lifestyle led to various personal problems, most notably alcoholism, from which he suffered for the rest of his life. These issues affected him on and off the field, often causing controversy.[9] Although conscious of his problems, he made light of them and was known for his intelligence and wit on the subject during periods of sobriety: "I spent a lot of money on booze, girls and fast cars – the rest I just squandered".[10] After football, he spent some time as a football analyst, but his financial and health problems continued into his retirement. He died in 2005, aged 59, from complications from the immunosuppressive drugs he needed to take after a liver transplant in 2002.
Early years and familyedit  
Best grew up on the Cregagh estate, east Belfast. The playing fields in the estate where he played football as a boy, Cregagh Green, is protected for community recreation in perpetuity as a Fields in Trust Active Space.[11]
George Best was born on 22 May 1946 in Belfast, the first child of Richard "Dickie" Best (1919–2008) and Anne Withers (1922–1978). He was raised in the Cregagh estate in east Belfast. Best had five siblings: four sisters, Carol, Barbara, Julie, and Grace, and one brother, Ian Busby Best.[12] Best's mother, herself an Irish hockey international, recalled that the boy was able to stand aged ten months and from then on was never seen without a ball at his feet, even taking one to bed.[13] His father was a member of the Orange Order and as a boy George carried the strings of the banner in his local Cregagh lodge. In his autobiography, Best mentioned how important the Order was to his family.[14] The Best family was raised in the Free Presbyterian faith.[15]
texts.4:
In 1957, the academically gifted Best passed the 11-plus and went to Grosvenor High School, but he soon played truant as the school specialised in rugby union. Best then moved to Lisnasharragh Secondary School, reuniting him with friends from primary school and allowing him to focus on football. He played for Cregagh Boys Club.[16] He grew up supporting Glentoran and Wolverhampton Wanderers.[17]
Anne Best died from alcoholism-related cardiovascular disease in 1978, at the age of 55.[18] Best's father died on 16 April 2008, 3 years after George's death, at the age of 88, in the Ulster Hospital in Dundonald, Northern Ireland.[19]
Club careeredit  
Manchester Unitededit
At the age of 15, Best was discovered in Belfast by Manchester United scout Bob Bishop, whose telegram to United manager Matt Busby read: "I think I've found you a genius."[20][21] His local club Glentoran had previously rejected him for being "too small and light".[22] Best was subsequently given a trial and signed up by United's chief scout Joe Armstrong. His first time moving to the club, Best quickly became homesick and stayed for only two days before going back home to Northern Ireland.[23] He returned to Manchester and spent two years as an amateur, as English clubs were not allowed to take Northern Irish players on as apprentices. He was given a job as an errand boy on the Manchester Ship Canal, allowing him to train with the club twice a week.[24]
Best made his First Division debut, aged 17, on 14 September 1963 against West Bromwich Albion at Old Trafford in a 1–0 victory.[25] He then dropped back into the reserves, before scoring his first goal for the first team in his second appearance in a 5–1 win over Burnley on 28 December.[25] Manager Matt Busby then kept Best in the team; by the end of the 1963–64 season, he had made 26 appearances, scoring six goals. Manchester United finished second, four points behind Liverpool.[26]
texts.5:
They reached the semi-finals of the FA Cup, where a defeat to West Ham United cost Best the chance to break a record. In the final Preston North End's Howard Kendall became the youngest ever player in a FA Cup Final – he shared the same birth date as Best.[26] That same season, Best captained the Manchester United side that won the 1964 FA Youth Cup, the sixth FA Youth Cup won under the management of Jimmy Murphy and the first since the 1958 Munich air disaster.[27]
The United Trinity statue of Best (left), Denis Law (centre) and Bobby Charlton (right) outside Old Trafford  
Rear view looking towards the stadium
Though opponents would often use rough play to try to stifle his technical ability, Busby ensured that "fierce, sometimes brutal" training sessions left Best well used to coping with tough challenges.[28] In the 1964–65 season, his first full season as a first team regular, Best helped Manchester United to claim the league title.[29] A 1–0 victory at Elland Road proved decisive as the title race came down to goal average between the "Red Devils" and bitter rivals Leeds United. Leeds managed to gain some measure of revenge though, by knocking Manchester United out of the FA Cup at the semi-final stage.[29] Over the course of the campaign Best contributed 14 goals in 59 competitive games.[29] He scored the opening goal of the 1965 FA Charity Shield at Old Trafford, which ended in a 2–2 draw with Liverpool.[30]
The rising star of English football, Best was catapulted to superstar status at the age of 19, when he scored two goals in a European Cup quarter-final match against Benfica at the Estádio da Luz on 9 March 1966.[31] His impressive stand-out display allied with his dark Beatle mop-top hair, the Portuguese media dubbed him "O Quinto Beatle" ("the fifth Beatle"); on the team's return to England, Best was photographed on the airport tarmac in his new sombrero with the headline, "El Beatle".[32][31] His talent and showmanship made him a crowd and media favourite and he went from being headline news in the back pages to the front pages.[31]
texts.6:
Before the game, manager Matt Busby had told his wingers, Best and Connelly, to stay deep for the first 20 minutes. Keep it tight and quieten the crowd. But George Best was only 19, too young for such caution. All he heard was 'blah, blah, blah'. When the game started, he grabbed it by the scruff. 'Watch this, Eusebio. And Coluna, Simoes, Torres, Germano, Jose Augusto. I'm George Best, and this is how it's done.'
— 'El Beatle' arrives, Jon Carter for ESPN.[32]
Other nicknames included the "Belfast Boy", while he was often referred to as "Geordie" in his native Belfast and "Georgie" in England.[33] However United failed to win any major honours in the 1965–66 season. Best was injured from 26 March onwards, with a twisted knee following a bad tackle from a Preston North End player.[34] United staff claimed it was light ligament damage, to keep Best on the field for the rest of the campaign.[34] He had little faith in the United medical staff and so he secretly saw Glentoran's physiotherapist, who readjusted his ligaments in a painful procedure.[35] His last game of the season, his knee strapped-up, came on 13 April, a 2–0 defeat to Partizan Belgrade at Partizan Stadium.[36]
The 1966–67 season was again successful, as Manchester United claimed the league title by four points. Best stated that "if the championship was decided on home games we would win it every season. This time our away games made the difference. We got into the right frame of mind."[37] An ever-present all season long, he scored 10 goals in 45 games. He then helped the "Red Devils" to share the Charity Shield with a 3–3 draw with FA Cup winners Tottenham Hotspur. It was the first game to be broadcast in colour on British television.[38]
texts.7:
Best scored twice against rivals Liverpool in a 2–0 win at Anfield and claimed a hat-trick against Newcastle United in a 6–0 home win on the penultimate league game of the season. However a home defeat to local rivals Manchester City proved costly, as City claimed the league title with a two-point lead over United. Yet the 1967–68 season was remembered by United fans for the European Cup win. After disposing of Maltese Hibernians, United advanced past Yugoslavian Sarajevo with a 2–1 home win. Best assisted John Aston for the first and scored the second himself and was described by Geoffrey Green of The Times as "the centrepiece of the chessboard ... a player full of fantasy; a player who lent magic to what might have been whimsy".[39]
In the quarter-finals, United advanced past Polish club Górnik Zabrze 2–1 on aggregate, having held on to their aggregate lead in freezing temperatures in front of 105,000 at Silesian Stadium. Despite losing the away tie 1–0, Best described the defeat as "one of our best-ever performances, given all the unwelcome circumstances".[40] Facing six times champions Real Madrid in the semi-finals, Best scored the only goal of the home fixture with a 15-yard strike that Alex Stepney described as one of Best's finest goals.[41] In the tie at the Bernabéu, Best was marked effectively by Manuel Sanchís Martínez, but on the one time Best got the better of him he made a telling pass[42] to Bill Foulkes, who calmly found the net,[43] to level the game at 3–3 and to win the aggregate tie 4–3.[44]
texts.18:
In an interview, Manchester United's Alex Stepney said: "Best would knock the ball on to the goalkeeper's shin, who would be rushing towards this feet to close down the angle, and the ball would bounce back to him and he would score. No one has been able to emulate that in football. Not only did he do it in training but he did it against Manchester United's arch rivals Liverpool at Anfield."[104]
The National Football Museum noted that Best played in an era of muddy pitches and heavy tackling, yet appeared to "glide through opponents" and could play on either wing, as a forward, or behind a central striker.[105] Writing for These Football Times, Jon Townsend highlighted Best's balance, strength on the ball, finishing and ability to slalom through defences, and argued that his game would have translated well to the modern era despite his having played without modern advantages such as sports science, nutrition, manicured pitches and lighter boots.[106] In a 2015 interview, José Mourinho, then manager of Chelsea, named Best as the player from any era he would most like to sign, describing him as "amazing" and "30 years ahead of his time".[107]
Personal lifeedit  
George Best's voice  
from the BBC Radio 4 programme The New Elizabethans, 20 July 2012[108]  
Problems playing this file? See media help.
During his early years at Old Trafford, Best was a shy teenager who passed his free time in snooker halls.[109] However, he later became known for his long hair, good looks and extravagant celebrity lifestyle, and he appeared on Top of the Pops in 1965.[110]
In 1969 Eva Haraldsted sued him for breach of promise, in the last such prominent case in England. However, the case never reached trial; instead, Haraldsted received a settlement of £500.[111]
Best had a brief relationship with actress Sinéad Cusack in 1971.[112]
texts.19:
He opened a nightclub called Slack Alice on Bootle Street in Manchester in 1973 and owned restaurants in the city including Oscars, on the site of the old Waldorf Hotel.[113][114] He also owned fashion boutiques, in partnership with Manchester City player Mike Summerbee. Best's cousin, Gary Reid, a member of the Ulster Defence Association, was killed in 1974 during an episode of serious rioting in east Belfast.[115]
"In 1969 I gave up women and alcohol—it was the worst 20 minutes of my life."
— Best quips on his lifestyle.[116]
Best married Angela MacDonald-Janes on 24 January 1978 at Candlelight Wedding Chapel in Las Vegas, having met her in the United States when Best was playing for the Los Angeles Aztecs in 1976. Their son, Calum, was born in 1981. They separated in 1982 and divorced in 1986.[117]
"If I had to choose between dribbling past five players and scoring from 40 yards at Anfield or shagging Miss World, it'd be a hard choice. Thankfully, I've done both."
— Best on life on and off the field.[118]
He married Alex Pursey in 1995 in Kensington and Chelsea, London.[119] They divorced in 2004[120] with no children. In 2004, she alleged that Best was violent towards her at times during their marriage, an issue that was covered in Best's authorised 1998 biography Bestie in which Alex claimed that Best punched her in the face on more than one occasion.[121] Earlier in the book it is revealed that he struck another of his girlfriends at least once and was arrested and charged with assault on a waitress, Stevie Sloniecka, in November 1972, when he fractured her nose in Reuben's nightclub, Manchester.[122] He was successfully defended when the case reached court in January 1973 by barrister George Carman QC, a close drinking companion of Best, as acknowledged in his book, Scoring at Half Time.
texts.20:
Although the football pitch was his arena, Best was essentially a pop star—young, stylish, strikingly beautiful, possessed of a creative confidence that bordered on arrogance, and worshipped by young men and women alike. Like The Beatles and The Rolling Stones, he epitomised the first, sudden, dynamic emergence of a postwar youth culture that, for better or worse, would help define the rest of the century. Long before Beckham, he was Britain's first footballer as popular icon.
— Sean O'Hagan in The Guardian on Best's celebrity status in the 1960s.[123]
At the peak of his career in the late 1960s and early 1970s, Best advertised Cookstown sausages on television with the phrase "the Best family sausages".[124] In 2007 a memorial plaque was placed outside the pork factory in the County Tyrone town.[124] In the early 1970s, Best also advertised eggs, under the campaign "E for B and Georgie Best", both in print and on TV, where "E for B" was short for "Eggs for Breakfast".[125]
Best had a cameo as himself in the 1971 British comedy film Percy. In 1984, he made a fitness album with Mary Stävin called Shape Up and Dance. The Farm's video for their 1992 cover version of The Human League's "Don't You Want Me" featured Best mouthing the chorus.[126] A biographical film entitled Best was released in May 2000, with John Lynch portraying George Best. Indie rock band The Wedding Present named their first album George Best and featured him on the cover wearing his red Manchester United kit. After his death, Brian Kennedy and Peter Corry released a single entitled George Best – A Tribute. Best features in EA Sports' FIFA video game series; he was included as an icon in the FIFA 19 Ultimate Team Legends.[127]
texts.21:
In 2007, GQ magazine named him as one of the 50 most stylish men of the past 50 years.[128] When Best played football, salaries were a fraction of what top players earn today, but, with his pop star image and celebrity status, Best still earned a fortune. He lost almost all of it. When asked what happened to the money he had earned, Best quipped: "I spent a lot of money on booze, birds (women) and fast cars. The rest I just squandered."[129]
In 2012, Best was featured in the list of The New Elizabethans to mark the diamond Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II. A panel of seven academics, journalists and historians named Best among the group of people in the UK "whose actions during the reign of Elizabeth II have had a significant impact on lives in these islands and given the age its character".[108]
Alcoholismedit
"I was born with a great gift, and sometimes with that comes a destructive streak. Just as I wanted to outdo everyone when I played, I had to outdo everyone when we were out on the town."
— Best on his excesses off the field.[130]
Best suffered from alcoholism for most of his adult life, leading to numerous controversies and, eventually, his death.[131] In 1981, while playing in the United States, Best stole from a woman by taking money from her handbag to fund a drinking session. He recalled the incident, "We were sitting in a bar on the beach, and when she got up to go to the toilet I leaned over and took all the money she had in her bag."[132]
In 1984, Best received a three-month prison sentence for drunk driving, assaulting a police officer and failing to answer bail. He spent Christmas 1984 at Ford Open Prison. Contrary to popular belief and urban legend, he never played football for the prison team. In September 1990, Best appeared on the primetime BBC1 chat show Wogan in which he was heavily drunk and swore, at one point saying to the host, "Terry, I like screwing".[133] In 2002, he told The Guardian: "I was ill and everyone could see it but me."[123]
texts.22:
Liver transplant and controversyedit
Best was diagnosed with severe liver damage in March 2000.[134] His liver was said to be functioning at only 20%.[135][136] In 2001, he was admitted to hospital with pneumonia.[137] At the end of July and start of August 2002, he had a successful liver transplant at the private Cromwell Hospital in London.[134] He haemorrhaged so badly during the operation that he nearly died.[138] The transplant was performed at public expense on the NHS, a decision which was controversial due to Best's alcoholism.[139] The controversy was reignited in 2003 when he was spotted openly drinking white wine spritzers.[131] On 2 February 2004, Best was convicted of another drink-driving offence and banned from driving for 20 months.[140]
Deathedit  
Gates of Belfast City Hall soon after Best's death, Another view.
Best continued to drink and was sometimes seen at his local pub in Surbiton, London. On 3 October 2005, he was admitted to intensive care at the private Cromwell Hospital in London, suffering from a kidney infection caused by the side effects of immuno-suppressive drugs used to prevent his body from rejecting his transplanted liver.[134] On 27 October, newspapers stated that Best was close to death and had sent a farewell message to his loved ones. Close friends in the game visited his bedside to make their farewells, including Rodney Marsh, Bobby Charlton and Denis Law.[141]
On 20 November, the tabloid News of the World published a picture of Best, at his own request, showing him in his hospital bed with jaundice, along with a warning about the dangers of alcohol with his message: 'Don't die like me'.[141] In the early hours of 25 November 2005, treatment was stopped; later that day he died, aged 59, as a result of a lung infection and multiple organ failure.[134][142]
texts.23:
Tributes were paid to Best from around the world, including from arguably three of the greatest football players ever, Pelé, Diego Maradona and Johan Cruyff.[95] British prime minister Tony Blair described him as "probably the most naturally gifted footballer of his generation, one of the greatest footballers the UK has ever produced".[143] Maradona commented: "George inspired me when I was young. He was flamboyant and exciting and able to inspire his teammates. I actually think we were very similar players – dribblers who were able to create moments of magic."[95] Fellow Manchester United legend Eric Cantona also paid tribute, saying: "I would love him to save me a place in his team, George Best that is, not God."[144] At Best's funeral, the Duke of York sent white roses bearing a message which described him as "an inspirational footballer from Northern Ireland whose skills captured the imagination of fans from around the world".[145]
The Premier League announced that a minute's silence would be observed before all Premier League games to be held over the weekend of his death; however, at many grounds a minute's applause broke out in his honour.[146] The first match at Old Trafford after Best's death was a League Cup tie against West Bromwich Albion, the club against which he made his debut for Manchester United in 1963.[147] The match, which United won, was preceded by tributes from former teammate Sir Bobby Charlton. Best's son, Calum, former teammates and surviving members from the West Brom team which he played against in his debut all joined the current United squad on the pitch for a minute's silence. During this, fans in every seat held aloft pictures of Best, which were given out before the match.[147]
Funeraledit  
The Best family grave at Roselawn Cemetery, overlooking east Belfast
texts.24:
His body left the family home at Cregagh Road, East Belfast, shortly after 10 am on Saturday 3 December 2005. The cortege then travelled the short distance to Stormont. The route was lined with around 100,000 mourners.[148] Former Northern Ireland manager Billy Bingham, international teammates Derek Dougan, Peter McParland, Harry Gregg and Gerry Armstrong and Denis Law were the first to carry the coffin to the base of the Stormont steps.[148]
There was an 11 am service in the Grand Hall attended by 300 invited guests relayed to around 25,000 mourners inside the grounds of Stormont. Best's brother Ian, agent Phil Hughes, Dr Akeel Alisa, who treated Best, and his brothers-in-law Norman McNarry and Alan McPherson, were also pallbearers. As the cortege left Stormont, the Gilnahirk pipe band played. The funeral was live on several television stations including BBC One. Afterwards, Best was interred beside his mother, Annie Mary Best, in a private ceremony at the hill-top Roselawn Cemetery, overlooking east Belfast.[148]
Memorialsedit  
Following his death, the George Best Belfast City Airport was named after him  
George Best waxwork in Malahide, Dublin
Belfast City Airport was renamed George Best Belfast City Airport as a tribute to Best.[149][150] The official new name and signage was unveiled to a gathering of the Best family and friends at the airport on 22 May 2006, which would have been his 60th birthday. Public opinion in Northern Ireland about the renaming of the airport was divided, with one poll showing 52% in favour and 48% against.[151] Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) deputy leader and East Belfast Member of Parliament Peter Robinson, in whose constituency Belfast City airport is situated, stated that his preference was a sports stadium be named after Best.[152]
"With feet as sensitive as a pickpocket's hands, his control of the ball under the most violent pressure was astonishing. The bewildering repertoire of feints and swerves... and balance that would have made Isaac Newton decide he might as well have eaten the apple."
— Sports writer Hugh McIlvanney.[100]
texts.25:
In March 2006, the airline Flybe named a Dash 8 (Q400) plane The George Best. The aircraft was later used to carry Best's family across to the Manchester memorial service for Best.[153]
In June 2006, Sarah Fabergé, great-granddaughter of Russian imperial jeweller Peter Carl Fabergé, was commissioned to create the George Best Egg, in tribute. A limited edition of 68 eggs were produced, with all profits from the sale of the eggs going to the George Best Foundation, which promotes health through sport and supports people with alcohol and drug problems.[154] The first egg is on display at the George Best Airport. For the first anniversary of his death, Ulster Bank issued 1 million commemorative £5 notes.[155] The notes sold out in five days.[156] The notes sold on the online auction site eBay for up to £30.[157]
In December 2006, the George Best Memorial Trust launched a fund-raising drive to raise £200,000 in subscriptions to pay for a life-size bronze sculpture of George Best. By 2008 the money had still not been raised until a local developer, Doug Elliott, announced on 29 January 2008, that he would put up the rest of the money and would manage delivery of the project.[158]

# Wednesday 22 May 2019
George Best statue gifted to Belfast on his birthday
*   [Home](https://www.irishfa.com/)  
*   [News](https://www.irishfa.com/news)  
*   George Best statue gifted to Belfast on his birthday
![Image 4: George Best statue.jpg](https://www.irishfa.com/media/24138/george-best-statue.jpg)
[](https://www.irishfa.com/news/2019/may/george-best-statue-gifted-to-belfast-on-his-birthday#)[](https://www.irishfa.com/news/2019/may/george-best-statue-gifted-to-belfast-on-his-birthday#)
Today a life-size bronze statue of football legend George Best was unveiled in Belfast on what would have been his 73rd birthday.
Belfast sculptor Tony Currie from the art group ‘Lecale Bronze’ created the statue, which was funded by fans through public donation. It captures Best’s famed movement and balance as he dribbles the ball.
The statue, which was officially gifted to Belfast City Council today, will be on permanent display outside Olympia Leisure Centre at the main entrance to the National Football Stadium at Windsor Park.
Accepting the statue on behalf of Council at an official unveiling ceremony, deputy Lord Mayor, Councillor Peter McReynolds, from Belfast City Council, said:“I’m delighted to accept ownership of this memorial to George Best, one of Belfast’s most well-known sporting stars and a footballer who is considered by many to be one of the game’s all-time greats.
"We are delighted to have worked closely with the Best family, Lecale Bronze, the Irish Football Association and the other parties who have come together to help make this happen.
“Given that George’s talents made him one of the country’s most well-known sporting stars, this statue will undoubtedly be a draw for visitors and tourists alike. Its location beside popular sport and leisure facilities and the main entrance to the National Stadium at Windsor Park will hopefully inspire future generations of young footballers to follow their dreams.”
Norman and Barbara McNarry said:“This amazing tribute to George is very special and one which live on for many generations.
texts.29:
# Wednesday 22 May 2019
“In July 1961, the road from Belfast took George to far off places and glittering heights. In December 2005, that road brought him back to Northern Ireland where tens of thousands lined the streets to say farewell.
“Today that road has finally brought our Belfast Boy home forever to the city, to the people and to the family who love him most of all.”
Belfast-born artist, Tony Currie from Lecale Bronze, who sculpted the statue said: “I would like to thank all fans for their donations to the project via our crowd funding appeal. They have hopefully enabled me to fulfil George’s wish to be ‘remembered for the football’.
"In completing this project we have always recognised that George faced difficulties in his life and that these were at times immense for both himself and those close to him.
“I would therefore like to record our thanks to Barbara and Norman for buying into our vision and supporting us every step of the way. I would also like to thank Belfast City Council for helping us manage this project throughout, and the Irish Football Association for all the help that they have given.”

**Tony Alexander Adams** (born 10 October 1966) is an English former [football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") player and manager. Adams played for [Arsenal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_F.C. "Arsenal F.C.") and [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team"), captaining both. Known as **"Mr. Arsenal"**, he spent his [entire playing career](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_one-club_men_in_association_football "List of one-club men in association football") of 19 years as a [centre-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre-back "Centre-back") there, making 672 total appearances and winning four English league titles. He is considered one of Arsenal's greatest-ever players[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-2) and is also included in the [Football League 100 Legends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_100_Legends "Football League 100 Legends").
With Arsenal, uniquely he captained a title-winning team in three different decades, won three [FA Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup"), two [Football League Cups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Cup "Football League Cup"), a [UEFA Cup Winners' Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Cup_Winners'_Cup "UEFA Cup Winners' Cup") and two [FA Community Shields](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Community_Shield "FA Community Shield").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-3) Adams is one of six people honoured with a statue outside the [Emirates Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirates_Stadium "Emirates Stadium"), Arsenal's home ground. He won 66 caps for [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") between 1987 and 2000 and played at four major tournaments.

When his playing career finished, Adams went into football management, spending periods in charge of [Wycombe Wanderers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wycombe_Wanderers_F.C. "Wycombe Wanderers F.C."), [Portsmouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portsmouth_F.C. "Portsmouth F.C."), [Azerbaijani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Azerbaijan "Azerbaijan") side [Gabala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabala_FK "Gabala FK") and Spanish side [Granada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_CF "Granada CF").
From early in his career Adams was an alcoholic. He was sentenced to four months in prison for driving while four times over the limit for blood alcohol, after crashing his car. From 1996 he recovered completely and became involved in helping sportspeople with drink, drug or gambling addictions by founding the [Sporting Chance Clinic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sporting_Chance_Clinic "Sporting Chance Clinic").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-interview24-4)
Born in [Romford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romford "Romford"), Greater London, Adams grew up in [Dagenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dagenham "Dagenham") and was a pupil at Hunters Hall Primary School from 1971 to 1978 and then [Eastbrook Comprehensive School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastbrook_Comprehensive_School "Eastbrook Comprehensive School") from 1978 to 1983.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-5) His cousin is fellow professional footballer [Steve MacKenzie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_MacKenzie "Steve MacKenzie").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-6)

### 1983–1989: Early career and Anfield title
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Adams&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 1983–1989: Early career and Anfield title")]
Adams signed for Arsenal as a schoolboy in 1980,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-7) and made his first-team debut on 5 November 1983 against [Sunderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunderland_A.F.C. "Sunderland A.F.C."), aged 17.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-:1-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-highs-9) He accidentally put his shorts on back-to-front before the match. Then, with virtually his first touch of the ball during the game, he gave it away, leading to Sunderland's opening goal. He put the ball into the opponents' net, but the goal was disallowed.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-:1-8) Adams became a regular player in the [1986–87 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986%E2%80%9387_in_English_football "1986–87 in English football"), winning his first major trophy that season when playing in the [Football League Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Cup "Football League Cup") Final win over [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") at [Wembley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-highs-9)
On 1 January 1988, he became Arsenal captain at the age of 21,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-greatest-10) remaining as club captain for the next 14 years until his retirement.

### 1983–1989: Early career and Anfield title
Adams's strong discipline of the defence was considered a factor in Arsenal winning the [League Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_Cup "Football League Cup") in [1986–87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986%E2%80%9387_in_English_football "1986–87 in English football") and then the [First Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_League_First_Division "Football League First Division") championship twice; the first in [1988–89](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988%E2%80%9389_in_English_football "1988–89 in English football") after a [win](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_0%E2%80%932_Arsenal_(26_May_1989) "Liverpool 0–2 Arsenal (26 May 1989)") over [Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_F.C. "Liverpool F.C.") in the final game of the season; the second in [1990–91](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990%E2%80%9391_in_English_football "1990–91 in English football"), losing once all season.

### 1989–1996: Arsenal's famous back four
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Adams&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1989–1996: Arsenal's famous back four")]
Together with [Lee Dixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Dixon "Lee Dixon"), [Nigel Winterburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Winterburn "Nigel Winterburn") and [Steve Bould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Bould "Steve Bould"), Adams was part of the "famous back four" that lined up in Arsenal's defence, which, under [George Graham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Graham_(footballer,_born_1944) "George Graham (footballer, born 1944)"), was renowned for its well-disciplined use of the [offside trap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offside_trap "Offside trap").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-11) These four remained formidable for over a decade. Arsenal notably conceded just 18 goals during their title-winning [1990–91 league season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990%E2%80%9391_Arsenal_F.C._season "1990–91 Arsenal F.C. season"), and the four players amassed over 2,000 appearances for the club.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-12)

### 1989–1996: Arsenal's famous back four
In [1992–93](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992%E2%80%9393_in_English_football "1992–93 in English football") Adams was the captain of the first English side to win the League Cup and [FA Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Cup "FA Cup") double.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-13) In 1994, Adams led Arsenal to their first European trophy in 24 years by defeating favourites [Parma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parma_Calcio_1913 "Parma Calcio 1913") 1–0 in the [1994 European Cup Winners' Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_European_Cup_Winners'_Cup_final "1994 European Cup Winners' Cup final") in Copenhagen.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-14). On 13 August 1994, he was rewarded with a testimonial at [Highbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_Stadium "Arsenal Stadium") against [Crystal Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Palace_F.C. "Crystal Palace F.C."). With an attendance of only 12,348, it was generally considered poor timing by the club.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-15)

### 1989–1996: Arsenal's famous back four
Despite this success, [alcoholism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alcoholism "Alcoholism") increasingly blighted his life from the mid-1980s. He was reportedly often involved in fights in [nightclubs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nightclub "Nightclub"), and on 6 May 1990 crashed his car into a wall in [Rayleigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh,_Essex "Rayleigh, Essex"); his blood alcohol level was found to be more than four times the legal [drink-drive limit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drunk_driving_law_by_country#United_Kingdom "Drunk driving law by country"). On 19 December that year, at [Southend Crown Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southend_Crown_Court "Southend Crown Court"),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-greatest-10)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-17) he was sentenced to four months in prison, and freed after half of his sentence on 15 February 1991,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-18) but continued drinking for another six years. Adams later said that in early 1996, aged 29, he was in a very dark period, not wanting to live when not playing football, unable to "do life". He suffered a serious knee injury in February that year and did not play for Arsenal again in the 1995–96 season.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-nyt1-19) One Sunday evening he drank seven bottles of [chablis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chablis_wine "Chablis wine"), so his (first) mother-in-law took the children.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-interview24-4)

### 1989–1996: Arsenal's famous back four
From mid-1996, with help from a man he named only as "James W",[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-interview24-4) he became one of the most high-profile [recovering alcoholics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recovering_alcoholic "Recovering alcoholic") in the UK;[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-ias-20) his battle with alcohol is detailed in his [autobiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autobiography "Autobiography"), _Addicted_, which was released in May 1998 to critical acclaim.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-ias-20)_BBC News_ reported in 2001 that he had become [tee-total](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teetotalism "Teetotalism").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-21)

### 1996–2002: Wenger's arrival and retirement
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tony_Adams&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1996–2002: Wenger's arrival and retirement")]
> "When I first came to Arsenal, I realised the back four were all university graduates in the art of defending. As for Tony Adams, I consider him to be a doctor of defence."
—Wenger hailing Adams' experience in 1997.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-22)
Six weeks into Adams's sobriety, [Arsène Wenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ars%C3%A8ne_Wenger "Arsène Wenger") arrived as Arsenal manager in October 1996. Adams reflected in 2020 that Wenger understood his psychology, and knew of the dangers of alcohol, as his parents ran a pub.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-23) Adams rewarded his manager's understanding handsomely, captaining the club to two [Premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FA_Premier_League "FA Premier League") and FA Cup [Doubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double_(association_football) "Double (association football)"), in [1997–98](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997%E2%80%9398_in_English_football "1997–98 in English football") and [2001–02](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001%E2%80%9302_in_English_football "2001–02 in English football").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-highs-9)

### 1996–2002: Wenger's arrival and retirement
In August 2002, just before the start of the [2002–03](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002%E2%80%9303_in_English_football "2002–03 in English football") season, Adams retired from professional football after a career spanning almost 20 years, his last match being the [2002 FA Cup Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FA_Cup_Final "2002 FA Cup Final").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-24) He played 674 matches for Arsenal (only [David O'Leary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_O'Leary "David O'Leary") has played more) and was the most successful captain in the club's history. The number 6 shirt that Adams wore when playing was not used again until the [2006–07 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006%E2%80%9307_in_English_football "2006–07 in English football"), when it was assigned to [Philippe Senderos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_Senderos "Philippe Senderos").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-25)
Just before his retirement as a player, Adams had applied to become manager of [Brentford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brentford_F.C. "Brentford F.C.") (who had just missed out on promotion to Division One) after the resignation of [Steve Coppell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Coppell "Steve Coppell"), but his application was rejected.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-26)

### 1996–2002: Wenger's arrival and retirement
Nicknamed "Mr Arsenal", he was honoured by Arsenal with a second testimonial game against [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_F.C. "Celtic F.C.") in May 2002 with many Arsenal legends playing, including [Ian Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Wright "Ian Wright"), [John Lukic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Lukic "John Lukic") and Adams's fellow back four stalwarts, Dixon, Winterburn and Bould. The game finished 1–1 with Lee Dixon, in his final appearance for the Gunners, getting their goal.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-testimonial-27) In March 2003, just seven months after his retirement and with Arsenal [BBC Sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Sport "BBC Sport") named Adams as the former Arsenal player that the club would most benefit from returning.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-28)
In 2004, Adams was inducted into the [English Football Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Football_Hall_of_Fame "English Football Hall of Fame") in recognition of his impact on the English game, and in 2008 he was placed third in the 50 Greatest Gunners poll on the club's website.
A statue of Adams was placed outside Emirates Stadium in celebration of the club's 125th anniversary on 9 December 2011. Manager Herbert Chapman and Arsenal's all-time top goal scorer [Thierry Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thierry_Henry "Thierry Henry"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-29) and later [Dennis Bergkamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Bergkamp "Dennis Bergkamp")[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-30) and Arsène Wenger,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-31) were also immortalised with statues outside the ground.

## International career
Adams made his debut for [England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_national_football_team "England national football team") against [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_men's_national_football_team "Spain men's national football team") in 1987,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-highs-9) and played in [UEFA Euro 1988](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1988 "UEFA Euro 1988") in West Germany. England lost all three games, but Adams scored in a 3–1 defeat to the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union_national_football_team "Soviet Union national football team"). He was the first player to represent England who had been born after the 1966 World Cup win.
After a highly promising start to his international career, Adams suffered a series of setbacks during the early 1990s. He was surprisingly left out of the [1990 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1990_FIFA_World_Cup "1990 FIFA World Cup") squad by manager [Bobby Robson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Robson "Bobby Robson"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-highs-9) missed [UEFA Euro 1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1992 "UEFA Euro 1992") due to injury, whilst England failed to qualify for the [1994 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_FIFA_World_Cup "1994 FIFA World Cup"). England reached the semi-finals of [UEFA Euro 1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_1996 "UEFA Euro 1996") as the host nation, before losing on [penalties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shootout_(football) "Penalty shootout (football)") to [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_national_football_team "Germany national football team").

## International career
Adams appeared at the [1998 FIFA World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_FIFA_World_Cup "1998 FIFA World Cup") in France. Later that year, he made headlines for several statements in his autobiography _Addicted_, criticising manager [Glenn Hoddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Hoddle "Glenn Hoddle") for his management of [David Beckham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Beckham "David Beckham") and [Paul Gascoigne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gascoigne "Paul Gascoigne"), and for making [Alan Shearer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Shearer "Alan Shearer") captain instead of Adams; he also called Gascoigne an alcoholic, which was denied by the player's representatives. Hoddle told the press that he had no problems with Adams's opinions from the book.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-32)
His international swansong was England's unsuccessful [UEFA Euro 2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Euro_2000 "UEFA Euro 2000") campaign in Belgium and the Netherlands. Adams started England's opening game against [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal_national_football_team "Portugal national football team") but suffered an injury during the match and missed the rest of the tournament.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-33)

## International career
With Shearer retiring from international football after the tournament, Adams regained the captaincy. However, within months, England lost a World Cup qualifier to Germany in October 2000, the match being the last to be staged at [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium_(1923) "Wembley Stadium (1923)"), before the stadium was demolished for rebuilding. That match was Adams's 60th Wembley appearance, a record. With [Sven-Göran Eriksson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sven-G%C3%B6ran_Eriksson "Sven-Göran Eriksson") eventually taking the helm and under increasing pressure for his place from the emerging and improving [Rio Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_Ferdinand "Rio Ferdinand"), Adams retired from international football, having made 66 appearances,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-34) before Eriksson selected his first squad. He was the last England player to score at the old Wembley Stadium when he scored England's second goal in a 2–0 friendly win over [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine_national_football_team "Ukraine national football team") on 31 May 2000. This was also his first goal since he scored in a friendly against [Saudi Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabia_national_football_team "Saudi Arabia national football team") in November 1988, thus making the record for the longest gap between goals for England.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## International career
Described as a "stopper" (or man–marking defender) by Tom Sheen of _The Guardian_ in 2014, Adams played as a centre-back. A tall, brave, rugged, physical, and committed defender, his main traits were his leadership, aerial prowess, and his ability to read the game and time his tackles. While initially he was not known to be the most gifted player on the ball from a technical standpoint, he developed this aspect of his game under Wenger, and he later excelled as a ball-playing centre-back, in which he became known for his ability to carry the ball out from the back, as well as his penchant for undertaking individual runs.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-testimonial-27)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-blindspot-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-39)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-oscuro-41) However, he was also known for his lack of pace.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Adams#cite_note-43)
